title: How 100 Starlings Took Over a Whole Continent
summary:
In the late 1800s, Eugene Schieffelin, a bird lover, set free about 100 European starlings in New York City's Central Park. He led a group that wanted to bring European plants and animals to North America. The plan worked too well. Within a few decades, the birds had spread across the country. By 1970, there were 200 million of them.

Scientists are puzzled. How did so few birds change so fast? One clue is microevolution, small changes that build up in a species over time. When a new group starts from just a few birds, it carries only a small sample of the first group's genes. Scientists call this the founder effect.

In 2014, researcher Zichello asked the U.S. Department of Agriculture for five starling specimens. They arrived in a box labeled Honey Baked Ham. She studied their differences in body shape and DNA. About two million starlings are killed each year by the USDA to protect crops and keep planes safe.

Starlings look almost the same, but small differences, bird by bird, show how evolution works in real time.
why_it_matters: It shows that even the birds you see in your own yard or park are still changing, and watching them can help us understand how all living things adapt.

keywords.explanation: Microevolution means small changes that build up in a species over time.
The founder effect happens when a new group starts from just a few animals and carries only a small sample of the first group's genes.
A specimen is one animal or thing collected so scientists can study it.
Genes are the tiny instructions inside a living thing that help decide how it looks and grows.
DNA is the material inside cells that carries the instructions for how a living thing grows.

background_read: A starling is a small bird, and long ago a bird lover named Eugene Schieffelin set free about 100 European starlings in New York City's Central Park because his group wanted to bring European plants and animals to North America.
The birds spread across the whole country, and because the new group started from only a few birds, small changes in their bodies built up over time.
Scientists study these tiny changes to learn how evolution works in real time.
Article_Structure: WHO: Eugene Schieffelin, a bird lover who led a group that wanted to bring European plants and animals to North America, and researcher Zichello, who studies starlings.
WHAT: About 100 European starlings were set free in Central Park, spread across the country, and changed little by little over time.
WHERE: New York City's Central Park, and then across North America.
WHY: Scientists want to understand how so few birds changed so fast, and what the founder effect and microevolution can teach us about evolution.
